title: Convert Sorted List to Binary Search Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: sequential BST insertion (unbalanced) versus divide-and-conquer construction using the middle element as root at every level.

content.title: Convert Sorted List to Binary Search Tree

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the head of a singly linked list where elements are sorted in ascending order, convert it to a height-balanced binary search tree (a BST where the depth of the two subtrees of every node never differs by more than one).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Since the list is already sorted, choosing its middle element as the BST root automatically satisfies the BST property (everything before it is smaller, everything after is larger) while also guaranteeing the two resulting halves are as close to equal in size as possible, which is exactly what keeps the tree height-balanced when applied recursively.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building a Balanced Family Tree from a Sorted Guest List
blocks.text: Picture a sorted list of ages, and wanting to build a balanced hierarchy where picking the middle age as a "root" person naturally splits the remaining guests evenly younger and older. Repeating this splitting process recursively on each half keeps the whole hierarchy balanced.

blocks.caption: Choosing the middle value as root, then recursing on the two halves, keeps the tree height-balanced

blocks.text: One valid height-balanced BST (shown here in preorder as root, left, right, with "null" for empty children): 0 -10 null -3 null null 5 null 9 null null. Root is 0, with left subtree rooted at -10 (right child -3) and right subtree rooted at 5 (right child 9).

Before inserting values one at a time (which risks an unbalanced, skewed tree when inserting already-sorted data), notice that since the input is sorted, always choosing the MIDDLE element as the current subtree's root, and recursing on the left and right halves, is the standard divide-and-conquer technique for building a balanced BST directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Inserting sorted values one by one into a plain BST (in ascending order) produces a completely skewed, linked-list-like tree, the opposite of height-balanced.

Observation 2: Instead, treating this as a divide-and-conquer problem, pick the MIDDLE value of the current range as the subtree's root, since it guarantees roughly equal numbers of smaller and larger values remain for the two subtrees.

Observation 3: Recursively applying this same "pick the middle, split into halves" rule to the left and right portions builds a tree where every subtree is balanced by construction.

Observation 4: Since a linked list does not support O(1) random access to its middle, either convert it to an array first (enabling direct index-based middle selection) or use the slow/fast pointer technique to locate the middle node in O(n) per recursive call.

This leads to converting the list to an array first (for simplicity and O(1) middle access), then recursively building the tree by picking the middle index as root and recursing on the left and right sub-ranges.
Insert each value from the sorted list into a BST one at a time, using standard BST insertion, without any special balancing.

items: For each value in the sorted list (in order), insert it using standard BST insertion (compare and recurse left/right).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Standard BST insertion is simple and correct for building SOME valid BST containing the values.
However, inserting already-sorted values in order produces a completely unbalanced (linked-list-shaped) tree, violating the height-balanced requirement.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) worst case, each insertion into a growing skewed tree costs O(current size).
Space: O(n) for the tree (though its height is O(n), not O(log n)).
Limitation: this produces a valid BST, but not a height-balanced one; explicitly choosing the middle element as each subtree's root guarantees O(log n) height, which is the actual requirement.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why sequential insertion fails the balance requirement: inserting already-sorted values always appends to the same side (e.g., always the right child), producing a tree with height O(n), not O(log n).

The divide-and-conquer fix: since the input is already sorted, convert it to an array (for O(1) index access), then recursively build the tree by choosing the array's MIDDLE index as the current subtree's root, recursing on the left half (indices before the middle) and right half (indices after the middle) as the left and right subtrees respectively.

Why this guarantees balance: at every recursive level, the two halves differ in size by at most one element, so the resulting tree's height is bounded by O(log n), satisfying the height-balanced requirement.

The core idea: divide and conquer, using the middle element as pivot/root at every recursive level, exactly like binary search but building a tree instead of searching one.

Convert the linked list to an array. Recursively build the tree: for a given sub-range, pick the middle index as the current root, recurse on the left sub-range for the left child, and the right sub-range for the right child.

blocks.caption: Recursively pick the middle index as root, splitting into two balanced sub-ranges

blocks.text: Because the source data is sorted, picking the middle index as root correctly places every smaller value in the left subtree and every larger value in the right subtree automatically, satisfying the BST property with no comparisons needed. Since the middle index always splits the remaining range into two nearly equal halves, applying this rule recursively guarantees the resulting tree has height O(log n), satisfying the height-balanced requirement at every node.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), converting the list to an array (O(n)) plus building the tree by visiting each element once (O(n)).
Space: O(n) for the array and the resulting tree, plus O(log n) recursion depth.

blocks.text: Convert Sorted List to Binary Search Tree is a direct application of the same "pick the middle, recurse on both halves" divide-and-conquer idea used in binary search, but constructing a tree structure rather than searching one.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "build a balanced structure from sorted data", think: divide and conquer, middle element becomes the root/pivot, recurse on both halves.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Sequential BST insertion runs in O(n squared) worst-case time and produces an unbalanced tree; the divide-and-conquer, middle-as-root approach runs in O(n) time and produces a correctly height-balanced tree.

items: Pattern: divide and conquer, using the middle element of the sorted sequence as the current subtree's root.
Core Idea: convert the list to an array, then recursively build: middle index becomes root, left half becomes left subtree, right half becomes right subtree.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for sequential insertion, O(n) for the divide-and-conquer approach.
Space: O(n) for both, but the divide-and-conquer approach also guarantees O(log n) tree height.
Most Important Observation: picking the middle element as root at every recursive level is exactly what keeps the tree height-balanced.
Interview Difficulty: an accessible, direct application of the binary-search "pick the middle" idea to tree construction.
One line memory trick: middle becomes root; recurse left half and right half the same way.
